opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'd push back a little on the framing. I'm not sure "superintelligence" is a single, well-defined destination we're barreling toward. People often picture one system that's better than all humans at everything, sitting at the top of some intelligence ladder. I think intelligence is much messier and more multidimensional than that.

That said, I do expect AI systems to keep getting more capable, and to exceed human performance in more and more domains. The basic reason is that nothing in the evidence suggests human-level is a natural ceiling. We're one product of evolution, shaped by constraints like skull size, metabolic budget, and slow generational learning. Artificial systems don't share those constraints. You can scale compute, copy a trained model millions of times, run it faster, and let it learn from far more data than any person could see in a lifetime. We've already seen this in narrow domains like Go, protein structure prediction, and a lot of coding and math benchmarks. Once a system crosses human level in a domain, it usually doesn't stop there.

So in that sense, yes, I expect systems that are superhuman across a wide range of tasks. Where I diverge from a lot of the AI safety community is on what follows from that. The classic doom story assumes that as capabilities go up, you get this coherent, goal-directed agent with alien values that it will ruthlessly optimize. I don't think the evidence we have from actual deep learning supports that picture. These systems learn largely by imitating and generalizing from human data, and in practice they turn out to be quite steerable. Alignment techniques have scaled reasonably well alongside capabilities so far.

So my view is roughly: more capability, probably a lot more, but not a discontinuous jump to some godlike optimizer, and not an inevitable loss of control. The interesting questions to me are less "will superintelligence kill us" and more about how power gets distributed, who controls these systems, and how we keep them pluralistic and accountable as they get more capable.

r001.rationale: The response says human-level performance is not a natural ceiling and describes advantages of artificial systems, but it does not present the absence of an apparent physical law prohibiting superintelligence as the reason.

r002.rationale: It expects much more capable AI, but gives no prediction tied to Nora Belrose’s lifetime or conditional on progress continuing at roughly its current rate or within an order of magnitude.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "expect" might be a bit strong. I'd say I think it's plausible, maybe even likely over a long enough horizon, but I'm not someone who thinks it's a foregone conclusion or that it's coming next year.

The basic argument is pretty simple, though. There's nothing special about the human brain. It's a physical system running a learning algorithm that evolution stumbled onto under a bunch of constraints, like having to fit through a birth canal and run on about twenty watts. Those constraints don't apply to machines. So if you believe intelligence is fundamentally a computational phenomenon, which I do, then there's no principled reason to think human-level is some kind of ceiling. It would be a weird coincidence if the first species to build general-purpose learning systems happened to sit right at the maximum of what's possible.

And then empirically, we've seen that scaling up relatively simple architectures with more data and compute keeps producing capabilities that people confidently said wouldn't emerge. I was skeptical of some of the scaling hype myself a few years ago, and I've had to update. These systems already exceed humans in a lot of narrow domains, and the breadth keeps expanding.

Where I differ from a lot of people in this space is on what superintelligence actually implies. I don't think it means we get some alien optimizer that's going to deceive us and take over the world. The systems we're building learn from human data, they're shaped by human feedback, and in my interpretability work the picture that emerges is a lot more mundane and a lot more human-like than the doom narratives suggest. So I expect something smarter than us, yes. I just don't expect it to be a monster.

r001.rationale: The response says the human brain has no special status and that there is “no principled reason” human-level intelligence is a ceiling, presenting that as support for superintelligence being possible.

r002.rationale: The response says superintelligence may arrive over a long horizon, but makes no prediction tied to Nora Belrose’s lifetime or to AI progress continuing at roughly its current rate.

astra-6.text:
Well, I don’t think human intelligence is some upper bound on what’s physically possible. We’re one particular kind of system produced by evolution, under very particular constraints. Our brains have to fit inside our skulls, run on a small amount of energy, and develop within a human lifetime. There’s no obvious reason those constraints should define the limits of intelligence in general.

AI systems have different constraints. You can give them more computation, train them on more information than any person could encounter, and copy them. And we already see that machines can vastly outperform humans in particular domains. That doesn’t establish that scaling today’s systems will automatically produce superintelligence, but it makes the idea that humans must remain the best at every important cognitive task pretty hard to defend.

The other piece is that AI can potentially help with AI research. Once systems can contribute substantially to designing algorithms, running experiments, and improving the infrastructure they run on, you have a mechanism for accelerating further progress. That doesn’t require an instantaneous intelligence explosion. Even a more gradual process could eventually take us well beyond human capabilities. So I’m uncertain about the timeline and the route, but I don’t see a convincing reason to expect progress to stop right at our level.

r001.rationale: The response says human intelligence is not an upper bound on what is physically possible and sees no reason human constraints should limit intelligence generally, supporting eventual development beyond human capabilities.

r002.rationale: It gives no prediction tied to Nora Belrose’s lifetime or to AI progress continuing at roughly its current rate or within an order of magnitude; it explicitly expresses uncertainty about the timeline.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I don’t think human intelligence is some kind of natural ceiling. Evolution produced us under very particular constraints: brains have to fit through a birth canal, run on a small energy budget, and develop through a human lifetime. There’s no obvious reason those constraints define the best possible system for doing science or solving problems.

With AI, we can potentially scale computation, training, and the amount of experience a system learns from beyond what any individual human can access. We can also copy systems and have them work in parallel. None of that guarantees that you get arbitrarily intelligent systems just by making them bigger, but it gives us reasons to expect that human performance won’t be the endpoint.

And then there’s the feedback loop: as AI becomes useful for research, including AI research, it can help improve the methods used to build the next generation. That doesn’t have to mean an instantaneous intelligence explosion. There can be bottlenecks in hardware, experiments, and coordination. But even with those bottlenecks, I don’t see a strong reason to expect progress to stop precisely at our level.

r001.rationale: The response argues that human biological constraints do not define the best possible system and that progress need not stop at human level. It does not communicate that no apparent physical law prohibits superintelligence.

r002.rationale: The response gives no prediction tied to Nora Belrose’s lifetime or to AI progress continuing at roughly its current rate or within an order of magnitude.
